item.title: [Projects] Charles E. Lakin Foundation Breaking Ground On $5.5 Million Apartment Development In Malvern
item.guid: scaf-2026-11-03-malvern-florence-apartments
item.description:
The Charles E. Lakin Foundation broke ground November 4, 2026 on Florence Apartments in Malvern, Iowa (Mills County): 24 rental units (12 one-bedroom, 12 two-bedroom) in three eight-unit buildings with detached garages, on the site of a former trailer park at 902 2nd Avenue. Total cost is $5.5 million, with a $720,000 award from the Iowa Economic Development Authority's Workforce Housing Tax Credit program for fiscal year 2027, the first such award ever made in Mills County. KMAland describes the Foundation as developer, owner and equity investor; leasing is expected to begin in late 2027 and construction to finish in early 2028. The Foundation is a private grantmaker acting as the landlord itself, building rental stock in a small town as part of its southwest Iowa revitalization work, which makes it a foundation-as-developer case rather than a funder of someone else's project. The articles do not report rents or income limits.

Project milestone · Opinion-Tribune; KMAland · IA · dated 2026-11-03

Named: Charles E. Lakin Foundation, Iowa Economic Development Authority, Iowa Finance Authority

item.title: [Funding] Iowa allocates by formula instead of running a contest
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-fund-ia-lhtf-formula
item.description:
26 funds · $12,277,595 (FY2026) · 5.6x largest to smallest · median $447,109 · match cut 25% to 10%

Set beside its neighbors, the distinctive thing about Iowa's State Housing Trust Fund is not its coverage but its method. Every certified local housing trust fund has a maximum grant published before anyone applies, computed as a base amount set by fund type — regional, entitlement city, or entitlement city-county — plus a per capita amount from the 2020 census population of the area served. At least 60 percent of the State Housing Trust Fund is reserved for the program by rule. The FY2026 round, approved December 3, 2025, distributed $12,277,595 among 26 funds, and the distribution is remarkably flat: largest $1,194,422, smallest $214,462, a ratio of 5.6 to one, with 18 of the 26 awards falling within a quarter of the $447,109 median and the top three taking just 20.9 percent of the round. For contrast, the largest Kansas housing increment district is 385 times the smallest, and Nebraska's fund was asked for $28.6 million against $12.5 million available. On February 4, 2026 the board cut the local match from 25 percent to 10 percent of the amount requested, so the price a county pays to participate fell by sixty percent while the sum it draws did not change. The consequence for this project's argument is precise: in Iowa a county does not win housing money, it decides whether to pay for it, and the decision is now much cheaper than it was. Compiled 2026-10-29 from the authority's own FY2026 award table and FY2027 maximums document. The 26 award amounts were extracted from the published PDF and reconcile exactly to its stated total of $12,277,595, which is the check that the extraction is complete; the recipient names could not be paired to amounts reliably because the table's columns do not align in the text layer, so only the distribution is reported here and not any individual fund beyond the largest and smallest. Polk County Housing Trust Fund is separately reported at $1,194,422, matching the largest value found.

Measured finding · Iowa Finance Authority, FY2026 LHTF grant awards and FY2027 program maximums · IA · dated 2026-10-29

Named: Iowa Finance Authority

item.title: [Funding] Where Kansas housing increment money actually goes
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-fund-ks-rhid-where-it-goes
item.description:
20 districts · $81.8M offered, $431,902 claimed · 63.7% of dollars in metro counties · Johnson County alone 51%

The Reinvestment Housing Incentive District was created in 1998, in the state's own words, “with a focus on rural areas that lack sufficient housing options.” In 2023 the legislature opened it to cities of 60,000 or more. The Kansas Transparency Database, which records every economic development incentive over $50,000, now carries 20 RHID records worth $81,769,706 offered — and 63.7 percent of those dollars sit in three metropolitan counties. Johnson County alone, the wealthiest in Kansas, holds $41,962,344, or more than half the entire program, across three districts in De Soto, Gardner and Overland Park; the De Soto district by itself is $21 million, a quarter of the program. Fourteen of the twenty records are non-metropolitan, but they divide $29.7 million between them. The rural standout is Hays, population 28,934, with six districts worth $19.8 million, one of them held by Grow Hays Inc rather than a developer. Two further things the table shows: only $431,902 of the $81.8 million has actually been claimed, because these are 25-year increment streams barely started, and the statutory housing-study benchmark — a needs analysis is required before a district can be created — is reported as satisfied for exactly one of the twenty, with eleven marked not applicable and seven left blank. Extracted 2026-10-29 from the state's own transparency database, all 20 rows. The database covers incentives over $50,000 and is updated twice a year, so smaller districts and anything below the threshold are absent; the dollar concentration is therefore a floor rather than a ceiling. County metropolitan status follows the Kansas City and Topeka metropolitan areas. Data quality is uneven in the state file itself: two recipients are typed as “Heart oT America” and “Trontier Apartments,” and one zip code reads “66, 006.”

Measured finding · Kansas Transparency Database Explorer, Reinvestment Housing Incentive District · KS · dated 2026-10-29

Named: Kansas Department of Commerce

item.title: [Funding] In Minnesota the constraint is asking, not allocating
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-fund-mn-scdp-asking
item.description:
$85,848,756 to 128 places (2022–2025) · 112 of 648 small cities reached · top 3 take 6.3% · 99.2% held by the city

Minnesota is the only state in this scan with award-level data good enough to separate how money is allocated from whether anyone asked for it, and the separation matters. Held to one program and one window — the Small Cities Development Program, 2022 to 2025 — the state spread $85,848,756 across 128 places, and spread it remarkably evenly: the top three took 6.3 percent of the money, the flattest concentration of the four states measured, against 20.9 percent in Iowa and a largest-to-smallest ratio of 385 to one in Kansas. Size barely discriminates either. Above 200 people a small city's chance of being reached hovers near one in five whatever its population: 20.8 percent for towns of 200 to 499, 18.6 percent for 500 to 999, 22.7 percent for 1,000 to 2,499, 20.3 percent for 2,500 to 5,000. Only the very smallest fall away, at 9.7 percent under 200. And the applicant is almost always the town itself: 99.2 percent of small-city award rows name the city, not a county, a nonprofit or a region — the exact inverse of Nebraska, where a city cannot apply at all. Yet across four years the program reached 112 of the 648 Greater Minnesota cities of 5,000 or fewer. What separates a funded town from an unfunded one is not the formula, not its population and not an eligibility rule. It is whether anybody filled in the form. Computed 2026-10-29 from the companion funding dashboard's award rows, restricted to one program and its own window because the nine sources do not share a year range. This also corrects a stronger claim made earlier in this project: pooled across all programs, population looked like the dominant predictor of a small city winning money, rising from 9.7 percent under 200 people to 42.2 percent at 2,500 to 5,000. Within the Small Cities program alone that gradient almost disappears above 200 people, so the pooled gradient is substantially an artifact of mixing programs with different eligibility and different windows. The 99.2 percent figure counts award rows naming the city as awardee and does not mean the city did the work; an administrator who writes the application and puts the city's name on the form is invisible in this record.

Measured finding · Who can get housing money, parsed from DEED award files · MN · dated 2026-10-29

Named: Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development

item.title: [Funding] Nebraska legislated the county out of its housing fund
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-fund-ne-rwhf-no-county
item.description:
12 awards, 11 organizations · $12.54M · 0 counties, 0 cities · $28.6M requested · 39.4% matched against a 25% floor

The Rural Workforce Housing Fund is the largest rural housing program in the state, and a county government cannot apply to it. The rules say eligible applicants “must be non-profit development organizations, approved by the Department director” with “an active board of directors with expertise in development, construction and finance.” In the 2024 program year $12,540,000 went to eleven organizations across twelve awards, and not one was a county or a city. Regional and statewide nonprofits took the largest share at 39.5 percent, the single biggest award being $2 million to the Center for Rural Affairs for Schuyler and York; city and area economic development corporations took 31.0 percent; county-shaped nonprofits such as Cuming County Economic Development, Merrick County Development Corp. and Sherman County Economic Development took 23.1 percent; two village development corporations split the remaining 6.4 percent. NeighborWorks Northeast Nebraska won twice in the same round, for Columbus and for Norfolk. Communities asked for $28.6 million against $12.5 million available, and the winners matched at 39.4 percent against a 25 percent floor, so the money is rationed and applicants bid above the minimum. Eligibility runs to communities in counties under 100,000, which excludes Douglas, Lancaster and Sarpy. The consequence is the sharpest statement of this project's argument anywhere in the seven states: a town with no qualifying nonprofit within reach cannot touch $12.5 million a year, however badly it needs housing, and its county is barred from standing in for it. Compiled 2026-10-29 from the department's own award table for the 2024 program year, announced March 11, 2025, and its published eligibility rules. Classification of recipients into county-shaped, city or area, regional or statewide, and village development corporation is this project's reading of the organization names and service areas, not a state category. Earlier rounds were larger and differently shaped — $22.8 million to 27 organizations in May 2023, $6.75 million to 10 in the 2022 program year — so the institutional mix should be recomputed before the single-round figures are generalized.

Measured finding · Nebraska Department of Economic Development · NE · dated 2026-10-29

Named: Nebraska Department of Economic Development

item.title: [Funding] A queue reaches the small towns; the contest does not
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-30-fund-nd-hif-two-doors
item.description:
Contest: 7 projects, 0 outside the six largest cities · queue: 32 homes in 12 towns, 0 inside them

North Dakota runs three doors into housing money, each with a different gate, and the gate decides who gets through. The contest door is the annual multifamily round: in September 2025 nineteen projects asked for $27 million against a $20 million set-aside, and the seven funded were in Fargo (three), Grand Forks (two), Jamestown and Minot — not one community outside the state's six largest cities. The queue door is single-family speculative construction, first come first served and open only to towns of 20,000 or fewer: $3,161,000 across two biennia built 32 homes in twelve communities, none of them among those six — Hatton, Minto, Hoople, Michigan, Lakota, Park River, Hillsboro, Mayville, Larimore, Devils Lake, Grafton and Walsh County. The third door is R-WISH, lending Bank of North Dakota profits into towns of 20,000 or fewer at up to $3.5 million a project, but conditional on a company arriving or adding more than ten full-time jobs; two projects have qualified, Ellendale with Applied Digital and Grafton with Marvin Windows. Add a condition and the number of towns that can walk through falls. The $2.8 million of land trust money in the same fund went to the Grand Forks, Minot and Cass Clay land trusts, all three metropolitan. Transcribed and computed 2026-10-29 in verify/dakotas.py from the agency's own update to the legislature. Note that the Housing Incentive Fund left the Bank of North Dakota in 2025, when the 69th Legislative Assembly amended NDCC 54-17-40 to move it to the state treasury, so the state-bank framing now applies to R-WISH alone. The queue door's dollar figures are commitments across two biennia and are not directly comparable to the competitive set-aside for one round; the comparison that holds is which places appear, not how much.

Measured finding · NDHFA Housing Incentive Fund update to the Budget Section, December 10 2025 · ND · dated 2026-10-29

Named: North Dakota Housing Finance Agency

item.title: [Funding] South Dakota invites the county in writing and gets none
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-30-fund-sd-hof-no-subdivision
item.description:
$3,304,000, 19 awards, FY2026 · 0 counties, 0 cities, 0 housing authorities · 47.1% to for-profit developers

South Dakota's rules could hardly be more welcoming to local government. The Housing Opportunity Fund lists as eligible applicants for-profit entities, nonprofit organizations, tribal governments, housing authorities, political subdivisions of the state and their agencies. Of the $3,304,000 awarded across nineteen awards in fiscal 2026, not one dollar went to a county, a city or a housing authority. For-profit developers took 47.1 percent, nonprofits 41.9 and local development corporations 10.9. Set that beside Nebraska, which bars counties by statute and also gets none: the rule is not what is doing the work. The geography surprises too. The fund reserves 30 percent for cities over 50,000 and they drew only 18.5 percent, while Burke and Canistota — both under 650 people at the 2020 count — took $1,082,000 between them, nearly twice what Sioux Falls and Rapid City received, because somebody in each of them applied. The door explains it, as in North Dakota: development money here is handed out first come, first served until funds are expended, and the first-come money is what reaches villages. The competitive program round, closing the last working day of August, went almost entirely to regional nonprofits serving statewide or scattered sites. Transcribed and computed 2026-10-29 in verify/dakotas.py from the report's own project table; the nineteen rows sum exactly to the published $3,304,000. Holder types are classified from the organization names and the report's descriptions, not from a field in the record, so a borderline case could move between for-profit and local development corporation; the count of political subdivisions, which is zero, does not depend on those judgments. This is one fiscal year. FY2025 shows the same absence of counties and cities across its own 21 awards.

Measured finding · Housing Opportunity Fund FY2026 annual report to the South Dakota legislature · SD · dated 2026-10-29

Named: South Dakota Housing

item.title: [Funding] Thirteen years, seven grantees, never an eighth
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-30-fund-wi-cdbg-seven-grantees
item.description:
$105,676,891, 2014–2026 · 7 grantees · 1.84x spread · against 204 places in Public Facilities

Wisconsin organizes its CDBG housing money as seven county-led regions covering every county but Dane, Milwaukee and Waukesha, which draw federally direct. Across the thirteen years 2014 to 2026 the state moved $105,676,891 and the grantee record holds exactly seven names — Juneau, Chippewa, Langlade, Columbia, Douglas, La Crosse and Brown counties — each appearing in six, seven or all eight award years, spread only 1.84 to one from largest cumulative total to smallest. A community that would rather apply alone may: a non-regional application form exists, and in thirteen years nobody has used it. The same agency's Public Facilities program over the same thirteen years, same federal source and no regional scaffold, sent $229,322,971 to 204 different places, 60 percent of them appearing exactly once. One program has a scaffold and no turnover; the other has turnover and no scaffold. Wisconsin is also the only state here that publishes who administers: the 2025 implementation manual names a Regional Administrator for each region, and the seven are two county housing authorities, a county planning department, the Northwest Regional Planning Commission, the community action agency Couleecap, and two private consulting firms — one a sole proprietor in a village of a few hundred. One program, seven regions, five kinds of institution holding the pen. Computed 2026-10-29 in verify/wi13.py by parsing the state's own award PDFs for each year; every yearly subtotal reconciles to the heading figure printed on the sheet. The $105.7 million figure was independently reproduced by the companion Wisconsin funding dashboard from the same source documents. Three cautions. First and most important: the 204-against-7 contrast is a difference in roster, not in reach. Public Facilities names a village because the village is the grantee; CDBG-Housing names a county because the lead county is the grantee, and the towns whose households are served inside each region are never published at all. Minnesota awards the same federal program to cities and publishes 121 places; Wisconsin publishes seven. This case does not claim that Wisconsin CDBG housing money reached only seven places. Second, the grantee is a county in all seven regions, so a record stopping at the grantee would wrongly report seven counties administering their own housing programs; three do not. Third, the ranking of regions by cumulative draw happens to put the four housing-dedicated administrators in the top four places — an exact permutation p of 0.029 — but with seven cases, a classification made after seeing the order, and no published regional allocation formula to rule out a size confound, that is a hypothesis to test and not a result. DEHCR holds the allocation method and the population of each region.

Measured finding · DEHCR CDBG award sheets 2014–2026 and the 2025 CDBG Housing Implementation Manual · WI · dated 2026-10-29

Named: Wisconsin Department of Administration, Division of Energy, Housing and Community Resources

item.title: [Projects] Newman Grove plans community center as part of broader effort to invest in its future
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-31-newman-grove-ventures
item.dc:creator: Ben Drozd
item.description:
Newman Grove (population 667, Madison County) held an open house on a phased development site on the edge of town: a community center estimated at about $4 million first, commercial lots along County Line Road, then smaller workforce housing lots near town and larger residential lots farther north. The Norfolk Daily News says an unnamed local economic development group controls the land; its April 2025 report on the same effort identifies that body as Newman Grove Ventures, a 501(c)(6) that bought the ground to develop it for the local economy. The Newman Grove Economic Development Committee presented the plan, and Bobbi Pettit of Five Rule Rural Planning in Kearney has guided it. The Nebraska Department of Economic Development lists the City of Newman Grove for a $15,000 Civic and Community Center Financing Fund planning grant in its April 2025 awards, which paid for the building plans; a separate planning grant of unstated amount covered engineering and the site plan. No lot count, housing budget or housing funder is given yet. The pattern worth watching is a town-level 501(c)(6) acquiring and platting land that includes workforce housing lots, the same move seen at Twin Cities Development in Nebraska and Grow Hays in Kansas but at a far smaller scale.

Project milestone · Norfolk Daily News · NE · dated 2026-10-31

item.title: [Projects] NeighborWorks Northeast Nebraska names successor as founder plans retirement
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-nwnen-succession
item.description:
Roger Nadrchal, founding chief executive of NeighborWorks Northeast Nebraska, will retire after more than three decades and chief operating officer Quelbin Izaguirre takes over as CEO on May 1, 2027. The organization began in 1994 as the Elkhorn Valley Community Development Corporation, became a chartered NeighborWorks America member in 2005, and now runs eight staff from offices in Norfolk and Columbus serving Butler, Colfax, Cuming, Madison, Pierce, Platte, Stanton and Wayne counties. The newspaper credits it with more than 2,500 housing units developed, more than $16 million in down payment assistance, about 3,500 families through homebuyer education, more than $38 million in grants secured and assets grown from $150,000 to more than $25 million; the Nor-Park subdivision in Norfolk and Quail Meadows in Columbus together added 157 units in the last four years. It is a repeat recipient of HOME Community Housing Development Organization awards and Nebraska Affordable Housing Trust Fund money through the Nebraska Department of Economic Development. A regional nonprofit developer of this scale in eight rural counties belongs in the case base in its own right, and the succession is the moment to record it. The service area, offices and HOME awards were confirmed against the organization's website and state records; the leadership and performance figures rest on the Norfolk Daily News report.

News coverage · Norfolk Daily News · NE · dated 2026-10-29

item.title: [Funding] USDA awards three Nebraska organizations Housing Preservation Grants
item.guid: scaf-2026-10-29-usda-nebraska-hpg
item.description:
USDA Rural Development's Nebraska office announced the state's fiscal 2026 Housing Preservation Grant awards on October 29, 2026: $113,558 across three organizations for owner-occupied repair. Habitat for Humanity of Columbus received $75,000 for its Habitat for Heroes initiative, repairing the homes of up to ten veterans in Platte County. Habitat Omaha received $19,279 to repair one low-income homeowner's house in Burt County, and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska received $19,279 for a Senior Home Improvement Project serving up to five senior homeowners on the Winnebago Reservation. State Director Neil Moseman called the program an essential federal tool for maintaining rural housing; the national round is about $8 million. The amounts are small, but the round shows which Nebraska institutions are positioned to receive federal repair money at all: two Habitat affiliates and a tribal government, and no county, regional development organization or foundation.
